This is a photo I took a few months ago, but I thought I'd submit it here to help as we try to get this subverse going.

This was shot 2015-03-30 at 9:06 PM Mountain Daylight Time in rural southeast Idaho. Temperature was around 60 °F, seeing was good.

Shot using my Celestron C90 (90mm aperture, 1250 mm focal length, f/13.89 focal ratio) with a Nikon D7000 at prime focus and a 2x barlow. Stacked about 200 frames. I processed the frames using PIPP for centering and cropping, AviStack for alignment and stacking, Registax 6 for wavelet sharpening, and Gimp for levels adjustment.

I think this is my best lunar shot so far (you can compare my previous attempts if you like). I'm quite happy with the focus and clarity in this shot. I keep going back and messing with the levels, because there's something going on with the levels/colors in Mare Imbrium that still doesn't sit quite right with me. But for the most part I feel really good about this attempt.

I'm happy to hear your thoughts and suggestions on what I could do better next time!

Voat Bourbon Review #1: Wood's Tenderfoot Whiskey

I'll preface this by saying I'm very honored to be the first to post a review over here.

Wood's Tenderfoot Whiskey

90 Proof
~$45

From their website:
>Tenderfoot Whiskey is our single-malt whiskey, aged in new American Oak barrels, and bottled at 45% (90 proof).

>Our Whiskey is made from a combination of three barley malts along with a small amount of malt rye and malt wheat to give it balance with a hint of smoke, chocolate and spice. Try Tenderfoot neat, or in your favorite whiskey cocktail.

Nose: Hint of smoke at first, but that disappears quickly. This smells strongly of a lumber yard, freshly cut young untreated cherry wood, some hay, with earthy notes and leather.

Palate: Raw cherry wood, there is a light sweetness (nothing distinct). Leather shows up mid-palate, with a cinnamon kick before reverting back to a dry woody flavor which sets us up nicely for the finish.

Finish: Sawdust, cherry wood, again, hay. Oh, wow, chocolate! The aftertaste is of dry lumber followed by chocolate again.

Notes: This is so unique. I'm not sure I wood (ha) pay $45 for a whole bottle of this, but I am super glad I got to try it. If you're a young wood fan, get this. I imagine if you're wood smoking some meats this would pair nicely. I'd also say the dark chocolate on the finish and in the aftertaste are just fantastic.

If you're interested in spotting/chasing, there are a couple of steps you take to become certified to spot/chase:

  1. SpotterNetwork - Create an account at Spotternetwork.org and take the first module under 'training'. It trains you on the basics of weather dynamics and how to 'read' the different conditions. It's actually pretty quick and very informative. Once you've completed the training you can send in what are called 'LSR's or Local Storm Reports to the Spotter Network. They forward the LSRs to the local NWS branch. This is the most basic level of spotting.

2: SkyWarn - SkyWarn is in-person training by the NWS. Training usually occurs around February/March of each year and is administered by your local NWS office. I HIGHLY recommend that you pursue your Amateur Radio Technician License prior to going to this. The Tech license is easy to get and about $15 bucks to take the test. You can get a handheld VHF radio off of Amazon for under $100. There is some studying involved to pass the test and if this is something you are interested in I can help you with the knowledgebase needed to pass/understand Amateur radio. I actually found it really stinking fascinating.

The reason I recommend the HAMM stuff PRIOR to Skywarn classes is because the Skywarn network uses the Amateur bands to do facilitate reporting and logestics. Most Skywarn radio repeaters are autopatched to the local NWS offices, so when you say "This is KE0EWX, I have a rotating funnel cloud 3 miles west of my position at 291 and 40 highway in Independence." The NWS office hears that report directly though their radio. Plus, we use the amateur bands to communicate and coordinate with each other in the field.

Also, having your amateur license opens up several other civil service opportunities. Most cities/towns have both ARES and RACES, which are both civil emergency management programs that operate using radio operators. When the really big storm hits, ARES does damage assessment (trees down in the road, power lines down, power outage reporting, structure damage, etc) There are classes for the emergency mgmt teams all the time.

You can still 'Spot' with Skywarn without having your radio license, but it's just a phone in process and the lines are usually packed with every yokel calling in 'funny lookin' clouds. We train so we know exactly what the cloud is and the context for it (I.E: A rotating wall clound = tornadic potential BUT DOES NOT = a tornado. A funnel cloud is MORE tornadic potential but still DOES NOT = tornado. A tornado ON THE GROUND = tornado. Keeping our reports accurate saves the NWS office tons of headaches when it comes to issuing warnings. It's why we exist.)

3: Additional Training - There are several online resources that help you hone your weather knowledge. Also, knowing the websites to keep tabs on and what maps to watch. (Storm Prediction Center's convective outlook, CAPE values for the region that map convective potential throughout the day, etc)

If you want to get your feet wet, I would recommend the following:

1 - Sign up at spotternetwork, take the training, become a spotter. Simple enough. 2 - Download RadarScope for iOS or Android. It's a paid app, but it's doing the job of a $200 desktop app, well worth the couple of bucks on mobile. RadarScope uses Lvl2 radar data (HiRes) and is what we all pretty much use on mobile platforms. You can plug your Spotter Network credentials into RadarScope and it will continuously report your location to the spotter network and let you see the location of other spotters. There is also an app called Rapid_Report that allows you to send in LSRs to the network.
